walkthroughs.body_html:
Pathogens include bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists.

Examples: TB (bacterium), HIV (virus), athlete's foot (fungus), malaria (protist). Each spreads differently — air, fluids, surfaces, vectors.

White blood cells called lymphocytes make antibodies that lock onto antigens. Phagocytes engulf pathogens directly.

Memory cells stay in the blood — a second infection triggers a faster, larger response = immunity.

Vaccines use dead or weak pathogens to safely train the immune system.

Antibiotics kill bacteria only. Overuse drives antibiotic resistance.

mcqs.q: How do vaccines protect you from a disease?
options: Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Vaccines kill the pathogen if it ever enters the body.
They expose your immune system to a harmless form of the pathogen so memory cells form, allowing rapid response if exposed later.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.

mcqs.q: What makes antibodies effective against pathogens?
options: Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Antibodies are general-purpose proteins that work against any pathogen.
Antibodies are tiny knives that physically cut pathogens apart.
They have a specific shape complementary to antigens on a particular pathogen, marking it for destruction or neutralising it.

mcqs.q: What does a gene code for?
options: Typically a polypeptide (protein) — through transcription to mRNA and translation by ribosomes.
A gene codes for a specific physical feature like eye colour directly.
Vaccines provide antibodies for life by adding them directly to the blood.
Each gene codes for an organ or body part as a whole.

mcqs.q: Approximately how many vaccines does the UK childhood schedule include by age 5?
A clinical trial gives one group a new drug and another group a placebo, with neither patients nor doctors knowing which is which. This design is called:
options: A double-blind trial
A field trial
An open trial
A single-variable survey

mcqs.q: Antibiotics are prescribed less often than before, partly to slow the spread of resistant bacteria. How does antibiotic resistance arise?
options: Random mutations make some bacteria resistant; these survive and reproduce.
Bacteria learn to resist after meeting the antibiotic.
Patients become resistant and pass it to bacteria.
Antibiotics create resistance genes in bacteria.

mcqs.q: A vaccine contains a dead or weakened pathogen. How does it protect against future infection?
options: It triggers memory cells that respond quickly on re-infection.
It supplies antibodies that last for life directly.
It kills any pathogen that enters the body for years.
It makes the body warmer to kill pathogens.

mcqs.q: Heart disease is described as a non-communicable disease. This means it:
options: Cannot be passed from person to person
Is caused by a virus
Always spreads through contact
Is treated only with antibiotics
